title: Reading files, streams and redirection
summary: cat, less, head, tail -f, and where output really goes.

steps.title: Reading files
body: | `cat file` | print a short file (or join several: `cat a b > c`) |
| `less file` | page through a big one: `/word` searches, `n` next, `G` end, `q` quits |
| `tail -f file` | keep printing new lines as they're written: **watching a live log** |
Never `cat` a 4 GB log: it floods your terminal. Use `less`, `tail` or `grep`.

steps.title: Three streams
body: Every process starts with three open streams:
Both 1 and 2 go to your terminal by default, which is why they look the same. Redirection rewires them:
| `2>&1` | stderr to wherever stdout points **right now** |
| `a \| b` | a's stdout becomes b's stdin |
| `/dev/null` | the bin: anything written there disappears |

steps.prompt: `ls` prints `notes.txt` to stdout and `ls: cannot access 'nope': No such file or directory` to stderr. What shows on the **terminal**?
steps.answer: ls: cannot access 'nope': No such file or directory
steps.explain: `>` only captured stdout. stderr still goes to the terminal; `notes.txt` went into out.txt.

steps.prompt: Which line sends **both** stdout and stderr of `build.sh` into `build.log`?
steps.explain: Redirections apply left to right. `> build.log` first points stdout at the file, then `2>&1` copies that. In the second option `2>&1` copies stdout while it still points at the terminal. (Bash also has the shorthand `&> build.log`.)

steps.prompt: Run the job, append normal output to `job.log`, throw errors away.
steps.explain: `>>` appends instead of truncating; `2> /dev/null` discards stderr.

steps.prompt: Will the file end up empty, or keep its old contents plus new ones?
steps.explain: `sort log > log` is a classic trap: the shell truncates `log` *before* sort reads it, so you get an empty file. Write to a temp file and `mv` it.
head keeps a b c d; tail keeps the last two of those.

steps.title: head and tail
steps.prompt: Write `List<string> Head(List<string> lines, int n)` and `List<string> Tail(List<string> lines, int n)` like `head -n` and `tail -n`. Asking for more lines than exist returns them all. Then write `List<string> HeadTail(List<string> lines, int from, int to)` that returns lines `from` to `to` inclusive (1-based), using the classic `head -n to | tail -n (to - from + 1)` trick with your two functions.
starter: List<string> HeadTail(List<string> lines, int from, int to)
solution: List<string> Head(List<string> lines, int n) => lines.Take(n).ToList();
List<string> Tail(List<string> lines, int n) => lines.Skip(Math.Max(0, lines.Count - n)).ToList();
List<string> HeadTail(List<string> lines, int from, int to) => Tail(Head(lines, to), to - from + 1);
hints: `Take` and `Skip` do most of the work.
Tail skips `Count - n` lines, but never a negative number.
template: Dojo.Eq("tail more than exist", dojoL, Tail(dojoL, 10));
